newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew commander ill before practice repairs.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew commander ill before practice repairs.

text.p: A Russian-American crew aboard the troubled Mir space station was scheduled to rehearse crucial repair work on Tuesday, despite uncertainty over the crew commander's health.

Russian Public Television said a special council of doctors would meet on Tuesday to discuss the condition of Vasily Tsibliyev. Mission Control said Tsibliyev was overtired and had cardiovascular problems.
A Mission Control official said a television link would be established with Mir at 1616 Moscow time (1216 GMT) on Tuesday.
It was not clear how long the link would last. On Monday Mission Control managed an unusually long, 60-minute, television linkup organised with the help of U.S. communication stations.
During the link Tsibliyev said he had been unwell since Mir collided with a cargo craft on June 25 and asked if he could take some medicine.
"It came as a surprise," Tsibliyev said. Mission control advised him not to take any medicine before the operation to repair the Spektr module which was holed in the June 25 crash.
"The main thing is not to worry. I cannot recommend any medicine for you. Try to rest as much as possible," a Mission Control doctor said.

Mission Control spokesman Valery Lyndin said Tsibliyev's general condition was within the norm and that the problem -- revealed during cardio-vascular tests on an exercise bike -- should not affect a planned sortie to Spektr later this week.
But more tests would be made on Tuesday and doctors would draw final conclusions then.
Flight commanders transmitted film to Mir on Monday for the crew to study ahead of the practice repairs.
The film shows cosmonauts going through the motions in a swimming pool -- the nearest available conditions to those in orbit -- with a commentary outlining the procedure step by step.

Flight director Vladimir Solovyov, said Tsibliyev and engineer Alexander Lazutkin had prepared their spacesuits for the dress rehersal in the undamaged Kvant-2 module. NASA astronaut Michael Foale will help them without a spacesuit.

"Now we have determined two dates for the sortie of the cosmonauts into the damaged module -- either the night of Friday to Saturday or night of Thursday to Friday. The final date will be known after the crew's training session," Solovyov said.
The repairs, expected to take six hours, are aimed at reconnecting power supply cables cut when the crew hurriedly blocked off Spektr after the crash sent air hissing into space.
